chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Muhammad ibn Yahya from Muhammad ibn Musa from al-Hasan ibn al-Mubarak from Zakariyya ibn Adam, who said:

I asked Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) about a drop of wine or intoxicating nabidh that fell into a pot containing broth and much meat. He said: 'The broth should be poured out, or fed to the people of the covenant (dhimmi) or to dogs, and the meat should be washed and eaten.'
I said: 'And if blood fell into it?' He said: 'The blood will be eaten by fire, if God wills.'
I said: 'What about wine or nabidh that fell into dough, or blood?' He said: 'It is spoiled (fasada).'
I said: 'Should I sell it to the Jews and Christians and make it clear (to them)?' He said: 'Make it clear to them, for they consider its drinking permissible.'
I said: 'Is al-fuqaa' in the same status if a drop of that falls into it?' He said: 'I dislike eating it if a drop of that falls into any of my food.'

key_terms.أَهْلَ الذِّمَّةِ: People of the Covenant (non-Muslims living under Muslim rule)
key_terms.الْفُقَّاع: Al-Fuqaa' (a type of flatbread or cake)
key_terms.نَبِيذ: Nabidh (fermented drink, often from dates or raisins)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on food contaminated by a drop of wine or blood in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* illustrates the Shia juristic principle of *katharat al-mukhallas* (abundance of the contaminant), where Imam al-Rida distinguishes between minor impurities in liquids or solids versus total corruption (*fasad*) in dough. It highlights the practical application of *istihlak* (dissolution) and the specific ruling for selling wine to People of the Book, reflecting the nuance between ritual purity (*taharah*) and economic utility in Shia fiqh. The mention of Imam's personal dislike (*karahat*) for consuming food contaminated by wine, even if technically permissible, underscores the emphasis on *ihtiyat* (prudence) in daily consumption.
